en: 12. Chapter on Seeing Akṣobhya (Part 4, End). Regarding the "Chapter on Seeing Akṣobhya": once the practice is perfected, one enters the realm of the Buddha and is able to see all Buddhas;
this chapter discusses this in full detail. Within it, the seeing of Śākyamuni Buddha is first clarified, followed by the seeing of Akṣobhya.
It is named "Seeing Akṣobhya" based on the latter. "Akṣobhya" is a term from the Hu language (Sanskrit), which here means "Immovable. This chapter...
Because one clearly perceives the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, this chapter is therefore titled "The Chapter on Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya.
A question is asked:
Since one also sees Śākyamuni in this chapter, why is it specifically called "Seeing Akṣobhya"?
Śākyamuni is constantly seen in this land, while the Tathāgata Akṣobhya is now personally beheld; thus, based on this new establishment, he is named "Beholding Akṣobhya.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni was seen in the preceding chapter, whereas the Buddha Akṣobhya is seen in this chapter.
Since this chapter first introduces Akṣobhya Buddha, it is titled "Seeing Akṣobhya.
Within this chapter, there is a fivefold analysis:

first, an analysis of the manifestation of virtues through Vimalakīrti; second, an analysis according to the Dharma; third, an explanation of the purpose of its inclusion; fourth, a differentiation from the preceding sections; and fifth, an exegesis following the text.
First, regarding how Vimalakīrti manifested his virtues:
those virtues are twofold.
First, the practice of liberation.
First, through the power of internal correct contemplation, one sees the Buddha of the Dharma-body;
second, through the function of liberation, the Buddha places [the assembly] in the wondrous Abhirati (Sukhāvatī), which is here translated as "causing this assembly to see.
The former is self-benefit, while the latter is benefit for others.
The manifestation of virtue is thus.
Next, in the second section, there is a classification according to phenomena (*dharma*).
Within this chapter, two types of phenomena are distinguished:
First is the cause as the means of accomplishment, which clarifies "seeing" in terms of the Dharma;
once the causal practice is perfected, one is able to enter the realm of the Buddhas because one sees all Buddhas.
Second is the fruit as the result of accomplishment, which clarifies the "Buddha" in terms of seeing.
The fruit of Buddhahood is difficult to manifest; it is manifested by relying upon what is seen.
Such is the manifestation of the Dharma.
Next, the meaning of the purpose [of this teaching] is explained through three successive gates.
There are two [aspects]:
first, an explanation based on vision (*darśana*).
The preceding chapter elucidated the essence of causal practice; as this causal practice increases, one is able to enter the Buddha-realm and perceive the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is discussed next.
Second, an explanation from the perspective of the Buddha.

The preceding chapter elucidated the cause; once the cause is perfected, the fruit is attained. Since the essence of this fruit is subtle and hidden, it is manifested by means of its manifestations, and therefore it must be analyzed.
The intent of this [passage] is as follows.
Next, the four gates are contrasted with the aforementioned [sections] to distinguish their differences.
There are three kinds of such differences, as has already been explained above.
First, the difference in the transformation of beings:
in the preceding chapter, the transformation benefited the Bodhisattvas of Various Fragrances; in this chapter, the transformation benefits the multitude of this Sahā world.
Second, the difference in the arising of illumination.

The preceding chapter elucidated the cultivation of one's own practice; as this practice increases through cultivation, one enters the realm of the Buddhas and is able to see all Buddhas—this is "superior progress.
Third, the differentiation of dharmas.
The preceding chapter elucidated the causes, while this chapter discusses the fruits; "fruit" refers here to the virtues of a Buddha.
Having thus distinguished the differences, the following five sections provide an exegesis according to the text.
This chapter has two parts:
first, the vision of Śākyamuni;
second, from "At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti" onwards, the clarification of the vision of Akṣobhya.
Within these two [instances], there are seven kinds of differences:
first, the difference in the person who sees.
In the former case, Vimalakīrti saw; in the latter, the great assembly saw.
Second, there is a difference in the Buddhas seen:
previously one saw Śākyamuni, and subsequently one saw Akṣobhya.
Third, there is a difference in the practice of the one who sees.
First, Vimalakīrti was able to see the Buddha because of his internal contemplation; later, the great assembly was able to see the Buddha through the power of their aspiration and seeking.
Fourth, the manifested body was different.

In the preceding section, Vimalakīrti, through the power of internal right contemplation, beheld the Dharma-body Buddha; in the subsequent section, the great assembly, by means of Vimalakīrti’s superior supernatural powers, beheld the form-body Buddha.
Because Vimalakīrti’s virtue is sublime, he is the Dharma-body; because the great assembly’s practice is inferior, they see the form-body.
Fifth, there is a difference in terms of universality and limitation:
within the preceding section, the vision is limited to seeing only the Buddha; in the subsequent section, one sees both the Buddha and his buddha-field.
Sixth, the difference in the accomplishment of practice:

In the preceding section, Vimalakīrti, through the power of internal correct contemplation, perceives the Dharma-body Buddha and accomplishes his own merit; in the subsequent section, Vimalakīrti, by means of supernatural powers, causes the great assembly to perceive the Form-body Buddha and accomplishes the merit of benefiting others.
7. Difference in the benefit of transformation.
In the preceding section, the transformed person abandons appearances to enter reality, accomplishing the practice of realization and attaining entry into the essence of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body;

in the subsequent section, the transformed person makes vows to seek birth [in that land], accomplishing the practice of teaching; therefore, the great assembly below, upon seeing the Land of Wondrous Joy, makes vows to seek birth there.
The two sections differ in these seven ways.
Within the first section, the Tathāgata initiates the discourse by means of a preliminary question:
"If one wishes to see the Tathāgata, by what means should one contemplate the Tathāgata?"
Vimalakīrti previously went from his own residence wishing to see the Buddha; he explained that this constitutes "wishing to see the Tathāgata.
To perceive the form of the Buddha according to its manifested appearance is called "seeing"; in reality, however, it is the internal realization in accord with truth that is called "seeing."
This was realized through internal awakening and vision, yet the great assembly did not yet know it; therefore, he asked to reveal it, inquiring, "By what means does one contemplate the Tathāgata?
Having thus manifested the body of Vimalakīrti, he caused the assembly to enter into the same realization as that which he himself had seen.
Within this, the first section—up to "observing the body as being like the Buddha"—briefly clarifies what is seen;
from "I observe" onwards, one observes that the Buddha is identical to oneself, extensively clarifying what is seen.

Question: Why not simply proceed directly toward the Buddha to clarify what is seen, rather than first observing oneself to categorize it by analogy with the Buddha? Answer: There are four reasons for this: 1. To eliminate arrogance: If one were to observe the Buddha’s marks and characteristics first, one might harbor thoughts such as, "The Buddha’s body is so sublime; how could I possibly attain it? This would lead to self-deprecation and discourage one from seeking the path. By first observing one's own body, one realizes that the Buddha was once an ordinary person like oneself, thereby removing feelings of inferiority and encouraging the aspiration to attain Buddhahood. 2. To establish a basis for faith: If one were to observe the Buddha’s marks and characteristics first, one might think, "Such a body is difficult to achieve; I am incapable of attaining it. This would cause one to abandon the resolve for enlightenment. By first observing one's own body, one sees that the Buddha’s body arose from causes and conditions, and that one possesses the same causal potential, thus strengthening one's conviction and resolve. 3. To facilitate understanding: If one were to observe the Buddha’s marks and characteristics first, they would be too profound and subtle to be easily grasped. By first observing one's own body, one can then gradually infer and understand the Buddha’s marks through analogy, making the teaching easier to comprehend. 4. To conform to the pedagogical method: The Buddha’s teachings often proceed from the familiar to the profound. By first observing one's own body, one uses what is near at hand to illustrate what is distant, employing a skillful means to guide the practitioner toward the ultimate truth. Thus, observing oneself serves as a preliminary stage for subsequently perceiving the Buddha.
First, it is because one wishes to lead people to seek the cause and thereby know the fruit;
by observing their own true nature, they may analogically understand the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Second, it is because one wishes to lead people to infer the cause based on the fruit.
This is because one knows that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is identical to one's own essence, and realizes the ultimate reality of oneself to achieve the path of Buddhahood.

Third, it is because one desires to lead others to know that the fruit and the cause are of the same substance and without distinction, seeking all the dharmas of the Buddha-Tathāgata within one's own body.

Fourth, it is because one desires to cause others to know that cause and effect are of the same essence and without distinction, thereby ceasing divergent views and realizing entry into the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Within the preceding section, the phrase "as when observing the true reality of one’s own body" means that one observes the cause as being of the same category as the fruit; because one observes the Buddha as being identical to oneself, it is said to be "as when [observing] oneself."
What is the reality of the body?
It refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the Buddha-nature, and the true self.
Because this is the fundamental nature of the body, it is called "real"; the essential character of this reality is designated as its "mark" (lakṣaṇa).
What are its characteristics?
They resemble those of the Buddha’s body.
To speak of it concisely, there are only three categories of meaning: first, suchness-emptiness; second, suchness-non-emptiness.
In the emptiness of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*), there are briefly two kinds:
first, emptiness defined as the absence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vivikta*); second, emptiness defined as the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vivikta*).

Regarding the absence of characteristics, as stated in the treatise: it is neither characterized by existence nor characterized by non-existence; it is neither non-existent in its characteristics nor non-non-existent in its characteristics.
It is neither of one characteristic nor of different characteristics; it is neither of non-one-characteristic nor of non-different-characteristics;

it is not the characteristic of both being one and different. It is neither its own characteristic nor another's characteristic; it is neither of non-own-characteristic nor of non-other-characteristics; it is not the characteristic of both being its own and another's.
All such conceptual discriminations of the deluded mind are entirely inconsistent with the realm of direct realization.

Regarding the "transcendence of nature": within the Tathāgatagarbha, there are all the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; these Buddha-dharmas share a single essence (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and are mutually constituted through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because they share this same essence, the particular is subsumed into the universal, and thus everything exists; yet when the particular is distinguished from the universal, everything is non-existent. Thus, the true Dharma is both eternally existent and eternally non-existent.
Now, to explain the absence of intrinsic nature so as to depart from [the misconception of] emptiness:
such is the meaning of emptiness.
As for what is called "not empty," although the dharmas within the *tathāgatagarbha* are immeasurable, they are briefly summarized as being of only two kinds:
First, form as it truly is; second, mind as it truly is.
Regarding form as it truly is, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha-nature is also form, and because it is form, it can be seen with the eye;

furthermore, as stated in that *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, sentient beings possess within them the faculties of the Tathāgata’s eyes, ears, and so forth, like images reflected across a horizontal mirror.
These are called "form as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-rūpa*); this is the dharma-gate of the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*) rather than the phenomenal matter of form.
What are its characteristics?

It is like the *asaṃskṛta-śīla* (unconditioned precepts) of a bhikṣu, or like the principles of the five elements and yin-yang; although their substance is form, they lack the characteristics of form. Because they lack the characteristics of form, they cannot be grasped as blue, yellow, red, or white, but instead apprehend the true form.
Although that which resembles it is material in essence, it lacks the characteristics of matter; because it lacks the characteristics of matter, the sages realize it.
The Dharma-body is formless, yet because its essence is material, the sages realize it as being fully endowed with all sense faculties.
Furthermore, because it is the gate of dependent origination of the nature of form, when realized by the sages, there is no condition under which it does not manifest.
As for the "mind as it truly is," this refers to the "True Mind" as described in the sutras.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges are integrated through dependent origination;

this integration constitutes the awakened mind’s intrinsic nature. Because of this knowing nature, when it conjoins with ignorance, deluded cognition arises; when ignorance is extinguished, it becomes right cognition.
This, too, is the realization of things as they truly are:
that the nature of mind and phenomena are identical and not insentient entities.
What are their characteristics like?
Just as a mirror reflects objects without discrimination, so too is the true mind:
although its essence is mind, it is free from discrimination. Because it is without discrimination, when the Sage realizes it, the [notion of] spiritual cognition is forever extinguished.
Because this is the nature of the mind, the Noble Ones realize it and possess the wisdom that knows reality as it is.
Because there is this cognitive nature of the gateway of dependent origination, the Noble Ones realize it and are fully awakened to all phenomena without exception.
This suchness of form and suchness of mind are called "not empty.
Suchness-emptiness and suchness-not-emptiness resemble the body of a future Buddha; therefore, they are compared to a Buddha.
"The same applies to contemplating the Buddha" means that one is precisely about to categorize [the Buddha] as being identical to oneself.
Since the Buddha and the Buddha-nature share the same essence while their attributes are distinguished, contemplating the Buddha’s body is thus realizing its identity with one's own true self.
What is the meaning of this?

Generally, the essence of all Buddhas is one; because their essence is one, when viewed from the perspective of the Buddhas who have received [this transmission], the essence of sentient beings has been eternally pure from the beginning, unobstructed and unstained—this is precisely the perfectly pure *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "The Buddha knows that sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvāṇa and do not undergo further extinction. Since this is the case for the further extinction of nirvāṇa, it is likewise so for the Buddha-body.

From the perspective of ordinary beings, that pure *dharmakāya* is obscured by afflictions; yet, as the basis for the pure qualities manifested later, it is called "Buddha-nature. Thus, it is of the same essence as the Buddha and without distinction.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of reality: that which is real regarding suffering, its origin, and so forth, is precisely the Tathāgata, the Buddha-nature, and space.

Furthermore, as it is said therein, the Three Refuges are identical to the self; because they are identical to the self, one contemplates the true mark of the body, and the contemplation of the Buddha is likewise the same.
From here begins the second section, which extensively explains how the contemplation of the Buddha is identical to oneself and what is seen therein.
Within this, there is first a detailed exposition followed by a summary.

Regarding the details, although the meanings are manifold, to speak of them briefly: it is wondrously transcendent of all marks while perfectly embodying all meanings; it is wondrously transcendent of all marks to the point that not a single mark remains, yet it perfectly embodies all meanings to the point that not a single mark is to be discarded.
The sutras state that the ultimate truth resides solely herein; to posit anything else apart from this is entirely false and delusory.
Therefore, the subsequent text says: "To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation."
Based on this ultimate truth, everything taught in the sūtras is identical to this.

Thus, within the ten merits of the Buddha’s Dharma-body elucidated in the "Vajra-body Chapter" (*Vajrakāya-parivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the characteristics of nirvāṇa are clarified; in the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*), its nature is clarified; and in the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*), the mindfulness of the Dharma and the Sangha—all of these are identical to this.
The praise of the Buddha’s Dharma-body in the *Amitābha Sūtra* is likewise identical to this.
Therefore, one should use what has been explained here as an analogy to reveal all truly real dharmas.
There are those who proclaim that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is merely emptiness and not existent; this is the "fixed emptiness" established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

To proclaim that the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya exists solely as non-emptiness is also the "existence of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva-sat) established by the non-Buddhists; it is not the Buddha’s dharmakāya.

Furthermore, some say that the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya is definitively neither existent nor non-existent; this too is a fixed definition established by the non-Buddhists; it is not the Buddha’s dharmakāya.

Others further claim that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body both exists and does not exist: it possesses true form and mind, yet lacks manifold characteristics; its existence does not constitute non-existence, and its non-existence does not constitute existence. This, too, is the "existence and non-existence" established by non-Buddhists, and is not the Buddha’s Dharma-body.

Others further claim that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body transcends the four propositions and is definitively ineffable; this, however, is the fifth "ineffable treasury" established by non-Buddhists, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*, and is not the Buddha's Dharma-body.
Free from these one-sided errors, all meanings are universally encompassed such that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-body.
Thus, when non-existence is spoken of as existence, that existence is not a fixed existence;
when existence is spoken of as non-existence, that non-existence is not a fixed non-existence.
That which is called existence and non-existence is neither existence nor non-existence; even "neither existence nor non-existence" is not a fixed nature.
That which is neither existence nor non-existence is spoken of as existence and non-existence; one should know that existence and non-existence, too, are not fixed natures.
These four phrases cannot be definitively described as "ineffable," yet that ineffability itself is not a fixed nature.
Since it is thus with the Buddha-body, so too are all analogous phenomena such as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and buddha-nature.
The text contains one hundred and two sentences in total, which may be grouped into three sections:
from the beginning up to "cannot be known by consciousness," it clarifies that although delusion is pervasive, wisdom knows that consciousness-knowing is itself a false conceptualization.
Second, from "without darkness" down to "all paths of speech are cut off," it clarifies the departure from provisional names, for names constitute the path of speech.

3. From "not a field of merit" down to "inexpressible and impossible to demonstrate," it clarifies the transcendence of verbal expression, because it cannot be manifested through verbal expression or conceptual discrimination.

Question: What is the difference between false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), provisional designation (*prajñapti*), and verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), such that they are separately described as being "detached"?
The state of emotionally grasping at things falsely is called false conceptualization.
The names applied to phenomena based on their characteristics are called "provisional designations" (*prajñapti*).
To rely on the arising of speech and discourse to explain all phenomena is called "verbal expression.
That which is fundamentally non-existent in reality is termed "detachment," and furthermore, the Buddha’s relinquishing [of all things] is also termed "detachment."
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, the analysis of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*) likewise transcends these three aspects.
Within the first section, the initial portion first reveals that the essence of the Buddha is devoid of characteristics, clarifying the transcendence of the grasped object (*grāhya*);

the final portion, stating that "it cannot be known by consciousness," reveals the transcendence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), clarifying the transcendence of the grasping subject (*grāhaka*).

Regarding the fourteen gates concerning the prior absence of marks (*animitta*), the first eight distinguish the Buddha’s essential characteristics through specific gates corresponding to various phenomena, while the latter six distinguish the Buddha’s essential characteristics through general gates corresponding to various phenomena.

Within the first eight sections, the initial six clarify that [the Buddha] is devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by demonstrating his non-existence; the final two reveal the reality [of his nature], manifesting that he is not non-existent.
Regarding the first six, the first explains the Buddha’s lack of characteristics by means of a teaching on the three periods of time.
It does not come from the past, nor does it go to the future; it does not abide in the present. The past, the future, and the present constitute the conditioned flux (*saṃskāra*).
Within this flux, one might come from the past toward the future, and in the interval between coming and going, one would abide in the present.
The nature of the Buddha’s body is eternally abiding, like space; therefore, it did not come from the past, it does not go to the future, and it does not abide in the present.

Elsewhere, it is frequently said that the "past limit" refers to the past and the "future limit" refers to the future. For what reason, then, is the past limit here termed "coming," which is inverted to "not coming," and the future limit termed "going," which is inverted to "not going"?
The commentary states:
"The three periods are their temporal divisions, distinguished in relation to phenomena (*dharma*).
Although time is defined in relation to phenomena, phenomena are always universal while time is always limited."

For example, when a single dharma of form (rūpa-dharma) extends across the three periods of time, it is termed "universal" (sāmānya); when those same three periods are distinguished individually, they are termed "limited" (pratyeka). The same applies to other cases.

Furthermore, time is the general (samudāya), while dharmas are always the particular (viśeṣa). A single present moment that subsumes many dharmas is termed "general," whereas the various distinct natures of those dharmas are designated as "particular."
As it is with the present, so it is with the past and the future.

There is this distinction between time and phenomena: if one takes a single phenomenon and divides it according to different times, that single phenomenon becomes divided into three phenomena according to the time.
Among those three dharmas, one part is past, one part is future, and one part is present.
Therefore, in the sutra, the former is called "past," the latter is said to be "future," and the current is designated as "present."

If one distinguishes a single universal dharma according to the three periods of time, one may say that this dharma comes from the past limit, abides in the present, and proceeds toward the future limit.
It is as worldly people say:
"I have come from childhood and am proceeding toward old age."

Therefore, in this context, "coming" (*āgati*) regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) is translated as "not coming," and "going" (*gati*) regarding the subsequent limit (*aparānta*) is translated as "not going.
The second [section] clarifies the Buddha’s detachment from signs by means of the dharma-gate that correlates with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
First, speaking with reference to form (*rūpa*):
"Not contemplating form" means not contemplating that the Buddha’s body exists as identical to form.
"Not contemplating suchness" means not contemplating that the Buddha’s body does not exist as identical to form.

Regarding "not observing the nature": the self-nature of form is neither existent nor non-existent; one does not observe the Buddha-body as being identical to that nature of form, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Within the Buddha’s equal dharma-nature body, there has never been form from the outset; based on what, then, could one say it exists?
Therefore, one does not contemplate form (*rūpa*).
Since form fundamentally does not exist, how much less could it be non-existent in relation to its counterpart? Thus, one does not contemplate the suchness (*tathatā*) of form.

When both existence and non-existence are simultaneously severed, there is nothing upon which to base a discourse of "neither existence nor non-existence"; therefore, one does not contemplate its nature (*svabhāva*).
As it is with the aggregate of form, so it is with the remaining aggregates.

The third section clarifies the Buddha’s state of being free from marks by means of the dharma-gate of the four great elements: "He does not arise from the four great elements; he is identical to empty space."
The fourth section clarifies the Buddha’s detachment from marks by means of the Dharma-gate of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

"The six sense bases have no accumulation; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind have transcended [them]"—to manifest that one does not create causes for the accumulation of constant effects is called "no accumulation."
Because that which previously existed has already been relinquished, it is said that the eyes, ears, nose, and so forth have already passed away.
The fifth point clarifies the Buddha’s detachment from marks by way of the dharma-gate corresponding to the three realms:
as the retribution of birth and death has expired, he "does not abide within the three realms."
The sixth section clarifies the Buddha’s state of being free from marks by means of the teaching concerning the three poisons.
Because the causes of birth and death have been exhausted through insight, it is called "the three impurities already abandoned.
Greed, anger, and delusion are termed the "three impurities"; since the Buddha has previously severed them entirely, they are said to be "already abandoned."
The preceding six sections clarify that the Buddha is free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
The following two sections reveal the Buddha’s actual attainment, demonstrating that it is not non-existent.
"Conforming to the three gates of liberation" clarifies that [his attainment] accords with principle.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the three gates of liberation; to realize and accord with them is called "conformity" (*ānulomika*).

Alternatively, the essence of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* shares the same substance as those three gates of liberation in its conceptual differentiation; because this sameness of substance is not contradictory, it is termed "conformity."
"Endowed with the three types of clear knowledge" reflects the perfection of his virtues.
Regarding the three types of clear knowledge, they are defined as the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows; the Buddha is fully possessed of all three.
The two types of bodhisattva-knowledge (*vidyā*), the Buddha-knowledge, and the knowledge of non-illumination (*avidyā*) are taught as three; the Buddha is fully endowed with all of them.

As explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, what is called "bodhisattva-knowledge" is the *prajñāpāramitā*, while what is called "Buddha-knowledge" is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*); these two refer to their respective essential natures (*svabhāva*).

"Non-illumination" (avidyā) refers to the eleven kinds of emptiness. Because emptiness is not itself the illumination of wisdom, it is called non-illumination; yet because it can give rise to the illumination of knowledge, it is also named "illumination.
This is like how the five sensory objects of the world are called the "five desires," because they can give rise to desire.
Although those such as Ignorance possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), they are devoid of conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is said that they are "equal to Ignorance.
The preceding eight [categories] manifest the Buddha-body by way of distinct gates corresponding to various phenomena.
The following six sections clarify the Buddha-body by way of a general approach that correlates it with all phenomena.
Since categories such as identity and difference apply universally to all phenomena, the first of these clarifies the principle of being neither identical nor different.
There are two meanings to this "explanation":
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding characteristics.
Since both identity and difference are utterly severed, it is therefore called "neither identical nor different."
Second, the analysis of the manifestation of virtues:

The essence, being replete with myriad virtues, is called the "characteristic of non-identity"; yet, as these myriad virtues perfectly constitute the essence—like the world’s empty space, unimpeded and immovable—it is not a separate entity in its entirety, and is thus called the "characteristic of non-difference."
The second clarifies that [the realization] is neither self-produced nor produced by another.
This explanation has two meanings:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding marks.
The absence of both self and other is called "neither self nor other.
Second, the classification according to its manifested virtues:

manifesting forms in accordance with transformation is called the "aspect of non-self," while the Dharma-body is quiescent and does not change according to conditions, which is called the "aspect of non-other."
Third, clarifying that it is neither non-existent nor grasped.
This also has two interpretations:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding marks.
Being and non-being are both transcended; therefore, it is called "neither non-existent nor grasped.
To say "not non-characteristic" means one does not cling to non-existence.
To say "not grasping at characteristics" means one does not grasp at existence.
Second, the analysis of manifesting virtues:

because he manifests forms according to those to be converted, he is not without marks; yet because his own virtues are eternally quiescent and free from discrimination, he is said to be "without grasping at marks.
Fourth, it clarifies that he is neither this shore nor the other shore, and so forth.
There are also two ways of explaining this:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions.
That "this," "that," and everything in between are all non-existent is what is meant by the phrases "neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor the middle stream," and so forth.
Birth-and-death is this shore, nirvana is the other shore, and the noble path is the middle; these are taught within the framework of the gates of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).
However, when sought according to ultimate reality, since birth-and-death fundamentally does not exist, there is no "this shore."
Since there is neither birth nor death, against what could one know that which is called "the other shore"?
Therefore, the preceding text states, "There is bondage and there is liberation.
If there were fundamentally no bondage, who would seek liberation?
Since both extremes do not exist, on what basis could one speak of a middle?
Therefore, there is no middle current.
Second, the differentiation according to the manifestation of virtues.
Because one realizes tranquility by relinquishing signs, one does not remain on this shore.
Because one attains great *nirvāṇa* without abandoning the world, one is said not to be on the other shore.
Because one practices both defilement and purity without being biased toward either, one is said not to be in the middle of the stream.
The fifth section clarifies how he transforms sentient beings.
Regarding the statement, "He contemplates quiescence, yet does not undergo eternal extinction," there are two interpretations:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding signs (*nimitta*).
Although he transforms sentient beings, he contemplates quiescent extinction and does not grasp at marks of existence.
Because he leads sentient beings into quiescence for the sake of their transformation, he contemplates quiescent extinction while transforming sentient beings.
Regarding "extinguishing without grasping," the meaning encompasses both aspects;
therefore, although it is said [to be extinguished], it is not eternally extinguished, nor does it cling to signlessness.
Second, the analysis of the manifestation of virtues.
Although one transforms through contemplation of stillness, this is the practice of entering stillness;
yet, because one does not undergo ultimate extinction, this is the practice of following existence.
The sixth clarifies that "it is neither this nor that."
There are also two ways of explaining this:
first, the elimination of conceptualization regarding signs.
This is not to be sought by referring to the body; for the Dharma-body is free from signs, and thus it is neither here nor there.

Furthermore, all Buddha-lands are entirely suchness (tathatā); there being nothing that can be designated as "this," it is called "not this," and there being nothing that can be designated as "that," it is called "not that.
To say "neither by this nor by that" is to distinguish [the matter] in terms of the mind.
It is for this reason that the true mind is eternally quiescent: because it does not act for the sake of this, it is said to "not by this";
because it does not act for the sake of that, it is said to "not by that."
Furthermore, all sentient beings are entirely non-existent; because there is nothing that can be done by this, it is called "not by this";
because there is nothing that can be done by that, it is called "not by that.
Second, the classification according to the manifestation of virtues.
The Dharma-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it does not reside exclusively here nor exclusively there. Therefore, it is called "neither here nor there.
Great Compassion covers all universally; it does not favor one over another. Thus, it is called "not by means of this" and "not by means of that."
The preceding section has clarified the absence of anything to be characterized by departing from signs.
The statement, "not grasped by wisdom, it cannot be known by consciousness," clarifies that by departing from deluded thought, there is no grasper.
Because the sages cannot comprehend it, it is called "that which cannot be known by wisdom."
Since it cannot be taken as an object of cognition, it is therefore called "that which cannot be known by consciousness.
Above, the first section clarified the departure from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Below, the second section demonstrates the departure from provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Within this, the beginning clarifies that the Buddha-body is free from characteristics, demonstrating that there is nothing to be named;
at the end, it states that all paths of language are cut off, demonstrating freedom from provisional names and clarifying that there is nothing capable of being named.
In the preceding section on the characteristics of detachment, there are eleven gates.
The first gate clarifies the Buddha’s detachment from characteristics by correlating it with the phenomena of light and darkness;
this explanation has two meanings:
First, the elimination of conceptual discrimination regarding characteristics.
Since both light and darkness are utterly transcended, it is said: "There is neither obscurity nor illumination.
Here, "obscurity" (huì) is synonymous with "darkness" (àn).
Brightness and darkness exist within the realm of mental states; since the True State is devoid of such states, it possesses neither obscurity nor illumination.
Second, the distinction of manifested virtues:
because true wisdom illuminates, it is said to have no obscurity; because actual realization ceases all conditions, it is said to have no ignorance.
Second, "without name and without mark" directly eliminates marks.
It is called "without name" because its essence is fundamentally non-existent; it is described as "without mark" because no shape or form can be apprehended.
Third, "neither strong nor weak" has two interpretations:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions.
When both strength and weakness are utterly transcended, it is called "neither strong nor weak."
Outside the essence there is nothing else; knowing this, against whom could one speak of strength or weakness?
Second, the distinction of manifesting virtue:
because the inner mind is humble and yielding, it is said to have no strength.
Because his virtuous conduct is lofty and supreme, it is said that he is "without weakness.
Fourth, regarding "neither pure nor defiled," there are also two interpretations:
first, the elimination of conceptual distinctions based on appearances.
When both defilement and purity are extinguished, it is called "neither pure nor impure.
If impurity were originally present, it could be removed to become pure;
but since impurity was never produced in the first place, what is there to remove that one could call "purity"?
2. The classification according to the manifestation of qualities:
that which manifests as the fault of defilement is called "impure," while its essence, being free from worldly defilement, is called "non-defiled.
5. Regarding "not abiding in a direction and not departing from a direction," there are also two interpretations:
First, the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding spatiality:
"Being apart from" means being non-existent;

thus, it is called "not abiding in a location. Since there is no location where it exists, it is called "not abiding in a location"; since there is no location from which it could be distant, it is called "not being apart from a location."
2. Analysis by way of manifesting qualities:
The manifestations emerging from the Dharmakāya are called "not abiding in any direction," yet these transformations where they appear are called "not departing from any direction.
6. Regarding "neither conditioned nor unconditioned," there are also two explanations:
First, the elimination of conceptual differentiation regarding characteristics:
when both characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are simultaneously transcended, it is termed "neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Question:
The Buddha always maintains that neither the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should be grasped as real; why then are they not so?
He explains:
According to reality, the conditioned is fundamentally non-existent; knowing this, against what could one speak of the "unconditioned"?
Therefore, it is also negated.
Second, the differentiation according to its manifested virtues:
because the Dharma-body is quiescent, it is not conditioned; because its wondrous functions arise profusely, it is not unconditioned.
Seventh, "Non-demonstration and Non-exposition": this merely eliminates conceptual signs.
To employ speech when addressing a person is termed "demonstrating," while to proclaim the Dharma through speech is termed "exposing."
Since the truth is ineffable, there is no demonstration or teaching.
Eighth, the Buddha-body is revealed by way of the six perfections and the six opposing dharmas.
There are three meanings to this interpretation:
First, the elimination of conceptual discrimination:
since the six perfections and the six opposing defects are entirely non-existent, it is said, "There is no giving and no stinginess, up to and including no wisdom and no ignorance in the sixth."
Second, the analysis according to the negation of characteristics to reveal qualities.
Within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), because there is no relinquishing in the ultimate truth, it is said that "there is no giving"; this phrase negates characteristics.
Because one practices giving in accordance with worldly convention, it is said that "one is not stingy"; this phrase reveals the quality.

Within the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), because there is no evil to be prevented from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called "non-discipline"; this phrase eliminates conceptual characteristics (*nimitta*).
Because one conforms to worldly conventions while remaining free from transgressions, it is called "non-violation"; this phrase reveals its virtuous quality.
Within the context of patience (*kṣānti*), because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) there is no insult to be endured, it is called "non-endurance"; this phrase eliminates conceptual signs.
Because one conforms with the world while remaining free from anger, it is called "non-resentment"; this phrase reveals its virtue.
Within the context of diligence (*vīrya*), it is called "non-advancing" because there is no cultivation regarding the ultimate principle; this phrase eliminates conceptual signs (*nimitta*).
It is called "non-laxity" because one exerts effort in accordance with worldly conventions; this phrase reveals its virtue (*guṇa*).

Within the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), because there is no mind that can be stilled in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is called "not fixed"; this phrase eliminates conceptual marks (*nimitta*).
Because one practices meditation in accordance with the world, it is called "not distracted"; this phrase reveals its virtue.

Within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because there is no wisdom to be cultivated in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is called "non-intelligence"; this phrase eliminates conceptual marks (*nimitta*).
In accordance with worldly convention, cultivating wisdom is termed "non-delusion."
This [first section] distinguishes by negating characteristics to reveal virtues;
the third [section] distinguishes solely by revealing virtues.
It shows that because they give rise to the fault of defilement, there is no giving and so forth; and because they constantly practice pure virtues, there is no stinginess and so forth.
9. "Not Deceptive and Not Deceitful": "Deceptive" pertains to the mouth; "sincerity" (cheng) means reality, while "deceit" (qi) refers to fraud.
Truthful speech is called sincerity; false words are termed deceit.
There are three meanings of "understanding" (*jie*):
first, the elimination of conceptualization regarding signs.
Since both "sincerity" and "deceit" are non-existent, it is termed "neither sincere nor deceitful," because it is beyond words.
Second, the analysis by way of dispelling characteristics to reveal qualities:
Within the true Dharma, because both [subject and object] are non-existent in reality, it is called "not truthful"; this is the dispelling of characteristics.
Because it accords with worldly conventional truth, it is said to be "not deceptive."
The third point distinguishes [the teaching] solely by way of manifesting its virtues.
Because provisional words are used to save sentient beings, it is called "not being insincere"; because true words are used to transform sentient beings, it is called "not being deceptive.
Tenth, "Neither coming nor going."
Regarding "coming and going" in relation to the body, there are two interpretations:
first, the negation of conceptual distinctions, wherein both coming and going are without name, thus they are "not coming and going";
second, the manifestation of conceptual distinctions, wherein the dharma-body is eternally abiding, thus it is called "not coming and going."
The eleventh section, "Neither Emerging nor Entering": Emerging and entering depend upon the mind;
following what has a name is called "emerging," while realizing and knowing it is called "entering.
There are also two ways of understanding this:
First, the differentiation of the elimination of characteristics: because both entering and exiting are entirely without name, there is neither exiting nor entering.

Second, the differentiation of the manifestation of virtues: because practice constantly enters into suchness, it is called "non-exiting"; because it constantly accords with transformation, it is called "non-entering."

The preceding section clarifies that the Buddha-body is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and even transcends all paths of verbal expression, thereby demonstrating that the Buddha is free from names (*nāman*).
Names are the basis upon which speech relies; thus, they are termed the "path of verbal expression."
Names arise from characteristics; since characteristics are fundamentally non-existent, upon what could names be bestowed?
Thus, all paths of language are cut off.
The above constitutes the second section, clarifying the departure from provisional names.
From here below is the third section, clarifying the transcendence of verbal expression.
Within this, the initial portion clarifies that the Buddha-body is free from characteristics, thereby demonstrating the transcendence of that which is spoken;
the final portion, through the indication of "inexpressibility," correctly clarifies the transcendence of words and demonstrates the transcendence of the speaker.
In the preceding section on "Detachment from Characteristics," there are sixteen gates.
The first is: "Neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit.
This explanation has two meanings:
First, the elimination of conceptual distinctions:
Since both "field" and "non-field" are entirely non-existent, it is called neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit.
It is not a field of merit because it does not resemble virtuous persons; it is not a non-field of merit because it does not resemble those who commit offenses.
Second, the analysis according to the negation of characteristics to reveal qualities:
The Dharmakāya is equal and has no recipient of offerings, which is termed "not a field of merit"; this is the negation of characteristics.
Because it manifests the acceptance [of offerings] in accordance with transformation, it is not "not a field"; this phrase reveals its qualities.
2. "Neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings": the two interpretations are the same as before.
3. "Neither grasping nor abandoning": grasping at purity and abandoning defilement are what is meant by grasping and abandoning.
There are two meanings of "understanding" (*jie*):
first, the analytical negation of characteristics (*xiang-fenbie*), wherein being free from both grasping and rejecting is termed "neither grasping nor rejecting.

Second, the analytical manifestation of virtues (*de-fenbie*), wherein not dwelling exclusively in attachment is termed "non-grasping," and because it follows both the defiled and the pure simultaneously, it is termed "non-rejecting."
Fourth, "non-characteristic and characteristicless.
Existence is called "characteristic," while emptiness is called "characteristicless.
There are two meanings to this interpretation:
First, the elimination of conceptualization regarding characteristics.
Seeking from the perspective of reality, characteristics are fundamentally non-existent; therefore, they are called "non-characteristics.
Furthermore, there is no "non-existence of characteristics" that can be maintained; thus, it is named "not non-characteristic."
2. Analysis by way of negating characteristics to reveal qualities:
Because the Dharma-body is eternally quiescent, it is said to be "without characteristics"; because its wondrous function accords with conditions, it is not "without characteristics.
5. "Identical to the limit of reality and equal to the nature of phenomena": This phrase is analyzed solely from the perspective of revealing the ultimate reality.

The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is identical in essence with that *bhūtakoṭi* and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because they are of one and the same substance without distinction, they are said to be "identical.
Sixth, "incalculable": this phrase refers exclusively to the elimination of conceptual distinctions regarding marks.
Words cannot reach it, for its name is ineffable;
the mind cannot grasp it, for its name is immeasurable.
It transcends the limits of calculation and estimation by worldly people; therefore, it is called "beyond all measure."
Seven: "Neither large nor small" has two interpretations:
first, the dispelling of conceptual distinctions; when both "large" and "small" are simultaneously severed, it is termed "neither large nor small."
2. Analysis by Way of Revealing Virtues:
It can be small yet not large, and it can be large yet not small; therefore, it is called "neither large nor small. 8. "Neither seen, heard, sensed, nor known":

visual consciousness arises accordingly as seeing; auditory consciousness arises accordingly as hearing; the [other] three consciousnesses arise accordingly as sensing; and mental consciousness arises accordingly as knowing.
This sentence refers exclusively to the elimination of conceptual discrimination regarding marks.
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is not like the six sense organs of phenomenal characteristics, nor is it like the objects of the six sense-fields; therefore, it is neither seen nor even known.
9. "Freedom from fetters and bonds" (visaṃyoga): this refers solely to the elimination of signs.
That all afflictions have been completely severed by the Buddha is called freedom from fetters and bonds.
Furthermore, according to reality, they have never existed from the beginning; this is called freedom from fetters and bonds.

Tenth, "Equalizing all wisdoms and being identical with sentient beings": because the true nature is equal and ordinary people and sages are one as such, one equalizes all wisdoms and becomes identical with sentient beings.
The eleventh gate, "Non-discrimination regarding all phenomena": whereas the preceding [gate] concerned equality regarding persons, this concerns equality regarding phenomena.
Because defilement and purity are equal, there is no discrimination.

The twelfth section, "All Are Without Fault, Without Turbidity, and Without Affliction," means that there is no fault in speech, no turbidity or confusion in mind, and no physical decay or affliction.
The thirteenth gate, “Non-action and Non-arising,” means there is no fruit to be produced and no cause to arise.
The fourteenth gate, “Non-birth and Non-extinction,” means that the essence is truly and eternally abiding; it has neither beginning birth nor ending extinction.

The fifteenth section, "Fearlessness, Absence of Sorrow, Absence of Joy, and Absence of Weariness": Since all characteristics of emotional states are entirely absent, there is no fear, sorrow, joy, or weariness.
The sixteenth section clarifies that "there is no past existence, but there is future existence and present existence.
Because there is no nature of arising that has already ceased in the past, it is not "already existing."
Furthermore, it is not that what was non-existent in the present begins to arise in the future; therefore, there is no "future existence.
Nor does it mean that what was originally non-existent comes into being now; therefore, there is no "present existence.
Thus far, we have extensively demonstrated that the Buddha-body is free from characteristics, clarifying that there is nothing to be taught.
"Cannot be indicated by any verbal expression" directly clarifies that it transcends words and demonstrates the impossibility of speaking of it.
Since speech arises based on characteristics (*nimitta*), and there are no characteristics to be discussed, how could one know what is being said?
Therefore, it cannot be fully expressed through speech or revealed through conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, all speech arises based on emotional sentiment; since emotional conceptions are fundamentally non-existent, who could give rise to discourse?
Therefore, it cannot be expressed or demonstrated.
The above has been a detailed examination;
below is the summary.
The statement "the body of the Tathāgata is such as this" concludes and clarifies the object of contemplation.
The section beginning with "acting in this way" concludes and clarifies the subject who contemplates.
"Acting in this way of contemplation" concludes that the contemplation has already been performed.
The section beginning with "By means of contemplation" below distinguishes the contemplation of false governance in order to cause others to attain correct awakening.
Above, Vimalakīrti beheld Śākyamuni Buddha;
from here on, secondly, Vimalakīrti uses his supernatural powers to cause the great assembly to behold Akṣobhya Buddha.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, Śāriputra asks Vimalakīrti from where he has previously come,
and the Tathāgata explains it for him.
2. When the great assembly heard this teaching and desired to see [the world], the Tathāgata sent [Vimalakīrti] to show it.
3. Vimalakīrti manifested it for them, and the distant palace of Abhirati was established within this land so that the entire assembly could see it together.
Fourth, when the work of transformation was completed, the land returned to its original place, and the great assembly saw this together.
Within the first section, Śāriputra asks the question first, and the Buddha subsequently provides the explanation.

Regarding the question asked by Śāriputra, "From where did you pass away to come and be born here? Śāriputra wished to cause Vimalakīrti to manifest his place of origin, so that the assembly might all see it together and resolve to seek birth there; for this reason, he asked him.
Below, Vimalakīrti rebukes his question to reveal that there is truly no arising, thereby causing the assembly to enter [the path].
Within this, there are three parts:
first, clarifying that the principle of non-arising based on the dharma attained by Śāriputra;...
Second, from "What do you think? It is like an illusion" onwards, it clarifies that phenomena are illusory to demonstrate that things are non-arising;
third, from "The one who perishes" onwards, it distinguishes the sage from the ordinary person to clarify that the self is non-arising.

Regarding the first three phrases of the preceding section: at the outset, Vimalakīrti poses a counter-question to Śāriputra, asking, "Does the defilement you have attained involve cessation and birth?
Here, "cessation" (沒) is synonymous with "extinction" (滅).

2. Śāriputra replied, "There is neither passing away nor birth. This is because the principle of emptiness and non-self realized by Śāriputra is not identical to the existence of phenomena; therefore, there is no birth or passing away.
3. Vimalakīrti answered by way of a paradoxical refutation:
"If the dharmas you have attained possess no characteristics of passing away or being born, why do you ask, 'From where did you pass away to come here?'"
In the second section, there are five distinct points.
First, Vimalakīrti raises an analogy as a counter-question:
"What do you think? For example, when a magician conjures up men and women through illusion, do they truly die or are they born? This is discussed according to their characteristics.
Karma is like a magician; because karma constructs the names of the six realms of existence, it is called "male" and "female.
Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental basis, the mind is like a magician; because the mind constructs all kinds of forms, they are called "male" and "female."
2. Śāriputra’s correct answer:
“There is neither death nor birth. Because illusions lack fixed reality, there is no arising or passing away.
3. Vimalakīrti cites the Dharma and poses a question.
1. "Have you not heard the Buddha say that all dharmas are like illusions?
2. Śāriputra replied, "Indeed, I have.
3. Vimalakīrti, summarizing his response, rebuked him in return.
"If all phenomena are like the nature of an illusion, why do you ask, 'From where did you pass away to be born here'?

In the first part of the third section, it states: "'Passing away' refers to the characteristic of the disintegration of deceptive phenomena; 'being born' refers to the characteristic of the continuity of deceptive phenomena. This distinguishes the ordinary person from the noble one.

"The Bodhisattva, though passing away, does not exhaust his roots of goodness; though being born, he does not increase his various evils. This passage distinguishes the Sage from the ordinary person and clarifies that he is subject to no birth.
From here below is the second section, wherein the Tathāgata provides an explanation.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the Tathāgata, in response to a question, identifies the place from which Vimalakīrti has come;
second, Śāriputra’s praise; [and third, the Buddha’s further instruction].
Third, Vimalakīrti, having offered his praise, clarifies the purpose of his arrival.
Within the first section, the passage "The Buddha told Śāriputra: 'There is a land named Abhirati and a Buddha named Akṣobhya'" precisely indicates his place of origin.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that Akṣobhya Buddha resides in the Land of Joy (*Abhirati*); here it is called "Wonderful Joy" (*Miaoxi*), which is largely similar in meaning.
The passage, "This Vimalakīrti passed away in that land and was reborn here," identifies his arrival from the perspective of the person.
Previously, Śāriputra asked why Vimalakīrti did not explain [the matter] himself, but instead caused the Buddha to speak.
The commentary states:
Previously, Vimalakīrti manifested that his own essence is truly without birth or death; now, people abandon [superficial] signs to observe and seek [the truth].

If he were now to say himself that he passed away from there and was born here, it would contradict what was stated previously; therefore, he did not say it himself, and the Tathāgata has explained it for him.
Second, within Śāriputra’s eulogies, there had been no comprehensive praise until now.
"This person is truly capable of abandoning a pure land to come and delight in this place of much anger and harm"—thus he praises him separately.
Third, within the section where Vimalakīrti reveals his purpose for coming, there are five distinct points:
first, Vimalakīrti asks, "When the sun rises, does it coincide with darkness?"
"Darkness" refers to obscurity.
Second, Śāriputra replied, "No," as a general answer;
then he answered specifically: "When the sun rises, there is no darkness."
3. Vimalakīrti asked again:
"For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?
4. Śāriputra answered.
"Desiring to use bright illumination to dispel darkness for them.
Fifth, Vimalakīrti briefly answers to reveal himself:
"A bodhisattva is thus," which corresponds to the previous day's discourse.
"Though born in impurity," it corresponds to practicing in Jambudvīpa.
"To transform sentient beings," it corresponds to clearly illuminating through desire.
"Not conjoining with folly," just as when the sun rises, there is no more darkness.
"Merely extinguishing the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings" is combined to mean the removal of obscurity.
This concludes the first section.
In the second section, it first clarifies that the great assembly hears the teaching and seeks to see [the Buddha], and subsequently, the Buddha dispatches someone to show them [the way].
Among those seeking to see [the Buddha], "those who thirst and yearn to see the world of Abhirati" seek to see that land;
"those who seek to see Akṣobhya Tathāgata and his bodhisattvas" seek to see those people.
Within the Buddha’s dispatching of [Vimalakīrti] to appear, the phrase "The Buddha knows what all those in the assembly are thinking" clarifies the reason for his instruction.
The statement "He addressed Vimalakīrti," etc., is the formal exhortation to manifest himself.
"Everyone desires to see" clarifies the reason for the exhortation.
These two sections are concluded.
Within the third section, first Vimalakīrti manifests the Land of Wonderful Joy, and subsequently the assembly sees it together.
When Vimalakīrti appeared in the midst [of the assembly], he first thought to himself:
"I shall not rise up from here, but will transport the Land of Wondrous Joy into this world.
Having formed this thought, he entered samādhi; as described below, he correctly took hold [of the land] according to his intention.

Regarding the initial phrase "neither rising nor sitting" mentioned above: it manifests the mastery of the Buddha-land, reveals his own power and capability, and demonstrates the virtue of inconceivable liberation.
The passage beginning with “the Cakravāḍa mountains of the Land of Utmost Bliss” cites the objects of apprehension, namely the land and its inhabitants.
Within this, the preceding section—“the world-system of Utmost Bliss has accomplished such immeasurable merits”—concludes it by way of a general summary.
"Reaching upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and downward to the surface of the waters" clarifies the limits of its reach.
"With his right hand," and so forth, reveals the manner of grasping the signs.
As it revolves in the hand "like a potter's wheel," it turns back and returns to this place.
It is called "Entering This Realm.
Not being startled by it even when provoked is like "Holding a Flower Garland.
Causing the assembly to see it together is called "Manifesting All."
Subsequently, taking up the middle [section] properly, there are four distinct points:
first, entering samādhi to take that [state] and place it here;
second, manifesting that the assembly possesses both awakening and non-awakening—first manifesting those who have awakened, and subsequently revealing those who have not.

In the preceding section on awakening, it was first shown that those multitudes requested the Taker and sought the Buddha’s protection; below, the Buddha answers them. It is not I, Vimalakīrti, who can know this through non-awakening.
Third, although the Wondrous Joy [Pure Land] enters this realm, it neither increases nor decreases.
Fourth, although the Sahā world accommodates that land, it is not cramped or constricted, remaining no different from its original state.
From here below is the second section, "The Great Assembly’s Common Vision," which contains five statements:
first, the Buddha’s observation.
"Behold, you all, the world-system of Abhirati," he said, exhorting them to behold that Buddha.
"Its land is magnificently adorned," he further exhorted them to behold that realm.
"The bodhisattvas' conduct is pure and the disciples are immaculate," he exhorted them to behold that assembly.
2. The great assembly answered in unison, "We have all seen it.
3. The Buddha observed their practice and instructed them:
"Those who wish to attain such a pure buddha-field should train in the path practiced by Akṣobhya."
Fourth, it clarifies that this assembly makes vows to seek rebirth there.
Fifth, the Tathāgata bestows a prediction upon them to strengthen their resolve to depart.
Verifying through these points, it is clear that this assembly also clarifies the Pure Land; it is not merely clarifying the body.
These three sections are concluded.
Fourth, first it clarifies that after the transformation is finished, the land returns to its original place; subsequently, it clarifies that the entire great assembly beholds this.
The text is explicit and thus easily understood.
The preceding three assemblies of individual sūtras are now concluded.
From the passage, "The Buddha told Śāriputra: 'Do you see the Buddha Akṣobhya of Abhirati,'" onwards, the general circulation [of the teaching] is clarified.
This circulation consists of two parts:
First is the observation of learning, practice, and dissemination;
second, from the section on "Entrustment" (*parindanā*) downward, it clarifies the entrustment and transmission of the teaching for its dissemination.
Since people must practice and the Dharma must abide, it is necessary to exhort them to study.
Since the Dharma-transmission teachings must flow on, they require entrustment.
Within the previous section on "Exhortation to Study," there are three parts according to the individuals:
first, exhortation to study through the relics;
Second, at the beginning of the "Chapter on Dharma Offerings," Śakra encourages study;
third, following the "Chapter on Dharma Offerings," the Tathāgata encourages study.
Since the encouragement to study by Śāriputra constitutes the propagation of the teaching, why is it expounded in this chapter?
Śāriputra said:
Because the Buddha asked, "Do you see the Land of Wonderful Joy?
Śāriputra replied that he did. He then immediately gave rise to a vow, rejoicing and congratulating himself, and encouraged others to study it; for this reason, this treatise was composed.
The beginning and middle have two parts:
first, "The Buddha said, 'Śāriputra, do you see the Buddha Akṣobhya of Abhirati?
Second, the response from "Śāriputra" onwards.
The answer consists of four points:
first, to manifest that one has already seen [the truth], he says, "Indeed.
Second, from the words "I pray that... downward, he gives rise to vows based on what he has seen.
1. "May all beings in every birth attain a pure land like that of Akṣobhya Buddha, and obtain supernatural powers like those of Vimalakīrti.
3. From "We are fortunate" onwards, [the text] expresses rejoicing in what has been attained by oneself.
The initial statement, "We have gained a great and wholesome benefit," is an expression of joy.
The phrase, "To have seen this person and to have approached and made offerings to him," specifies the matter for which there is cause for celebration.
IV. From "As for those sentient beings, whether now present... onwards, there is the formal exhortation to practice and study.
Within this, there are seven phrases:

"Those sentient beings, whether in the present or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who hear this sutra shall also obtain excellent benefit; how much more so those who, having heard it, believe, understand, and accept it," etc. This is the first phrase, clarifying the benefit for those who hear it.
Because the benefit is identical to one's own, it is said that "one also obtains" it.
Alternatively, this phrase may highlight the superior by citing the inferior, clarifying the benefit of practice.
The passage beginning with "If there is anyone who obtains this sutra with their hands" constitutes the second phrase, clarifying the benefit of obtaining the sutra.
The passage beginning with "If there are those who read, recite, and explain" constitutes the third phrase, clarifying the benefits of such reading, recitation, and explanation.
"Being protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" refers to these very benefits.
The passage beginning with "Those who make offerings to such a person as this" constitutes the fourth line, clarifying the benefits of making offerings to Vimalakīrti.
This is because Vimalakīrti’s essence is identical to that of the Buddha; therefore, to offer to Vimalakīrti is to offer to the Buddha.
Furthermore, making offerings to those who recite and chant before [the scripture] is equivalent to making offerings to the Buddha, for it is through them that the Buddha-dharma is transmitted.
The section beginning with "Those who write" constitutes the fifth phrase, clarifying the response regarding the transcription of the scriptural scrolls.
Because this section clarifies the Buddha’s Dharma-body, it is said that "the room where this sutra is written contains the Tathāgata.
The passage beginning with "If one hears this sutra and can rejoice in it" constitutes the sixth phrase, concerning the benefit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
"By hearing this sutra and rejoicing in it, one will not be far from attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is called 'Attaining All-Knowledge' (*sarvajñatā*).
From the passage "If one can believe and understand this sutra" onwards is the seventh section, clarifying the benefit of proclaiming it for the sake of transformation.

"One who believes and understands this sutra, and even expounds a single four-line verse for others, should be known as a person who has received the prediction of enlightenment (bodhi-vyākaraṇa)," because the Buddha is certain that such a person will become a buddha.
If even a single verse is thus, how much more so this entire section? Section 13:
"Dharma-Offering" (Part 4, End). Regarding the "Dharma-Offering" section: the following clarifies that Śakra-devendra and the Tathāgata exhort [the practitioner] to study.

In the "Exhortation" section, it clarifies practicing in accordance with the Dharma; because this follows the noble intention of the Tathāgata and is termed "Dharma-offering," this chapter is designated accordingly and is thus named the "Chapter on the Dharma-offering."

This Dharma-offering is called the "offering of practice" (*caryā-pūjā*) in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, and is termed the "offering of the path leading to the destination" (*yogasthāna-mārga-pūjā*) in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya* (or *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃgraha*).
Although the names have been altered, their meaning does not differ.
Within this chapter, the first part clarifies how the Heavenly King encourages the study and dissemination [of the sutra];
the second part, beginning with "This sutra extensively explains the Buddhas of the past, future, and present," clarifies how the Tathāgata encourages study.
In the first part of the middle section, the Deva-Indra encourages study; from the words "The Buddha said, 'Excellent'" onwards, the Tathāgata provides a descriptive praise.
Within the Deva-Indra’s encouragement, the text is divided into three parts:
first, praising the excellence of the sutra to cause people to cherish and delight in it.
Second, from "As I understand it" onwards, it clarifies the manifold benefits of study to encourage people to practice it.
Third, from "If there are those who have attachment" onwards, Śakra reveals his own offerings and protection to inspire people to hold [the teaching] in high esteem and reverence.
At the beginning, "At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra" introduces the person who extols the sūtra; this is an alternative name for the Lord of Devas (Indra).
"In the midst of the great assembly" clarifies the place where he extols the sūtra.
The phrase "He addressed the Buddha" and so forth serves to highlight the words of praise for the sutra.
The statement "Although I have heard hundreds of thousands of sutras from the Buddha" sets forth the inferior to manifest the superior.
The passage "I have never before heard this inconceivable [teaching]" and so forth contrasts the inferior with the superior to manifest its excellence.
As this sūtra describes the inconceivable virtues of Vimalakīrti, it is titled the *Acintya-ṛddhi-sūtra* (Sūtra of Inconceivable Supernatural Powers).
Furthermore, as this sūtra proclaims the definitive, true meaning of all phenomena, it is titled the *Niścita-tattva-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Definitive True Characteristic).
In the second section, the phrase "As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught" expresses his own understanding and clarifies the manifold benefits of study.
There are two kinds of benefit:
first, the benefit of receiving and upholding the teachings according to the sūtras;...
2. From "How much more so" (*kaḥ punar vādaḥ*) onwards, the benefits of practicing according to the meaning of the sūtra are clarified.
Within the preceding section, the phrase "if there are those who hear, believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, and recite it" identifies the person who upholds the sūtra.

"Will certainly attain it without doubt" clarifies the benefit of upholding the sutra; that is, one will certainly attain the inconceivable method of liberation taught within this sutra without doubt.
Regarding the benefit of practice, the initial phrase "how much more so for those who practice according to the teaching" uses the inferior to illustrate the superior.
Next, we shall discuss the benefits.
These benefits vary according to the respective stages; thus, they are discussed from both the lower and upper perspectives.

"This person then closes the gates to the evil destinies and opens the doors to all wholesome paths" refers to the benefit of the wholesome destinies prior to the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Relying on the sūtras to abandon faults is called "closing the gates to the evil realms"; relying on the sūtras to cultivate goodness is called "opening the gates to the wholesome.
"Constantly protected by the Buddhas" refers to the benefits obtained within the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Because the Buddha proclaims and establishes [the path], one receives the Buddha’s protection (*buddharakṣā*).
Protection causes one to depart from faults, while mindfulness causes the increase of goodness.
"Subduing external teachings, destroying the enmity of Māra, and cultivating Bodhi" refers to the benefits obtained from the first bhūmi upward.
Subduing outsiders and crushing Māras constitutes the benefit of destroying heterodoxy, which is also the benefit of benefiting others.
Because he possesses correct wisdom, he destroys the non-Buddhists; because he possesses the supreme path, he is able to crush Māras.
Cultivating the path to enlightenment is to abide in correct benefit, which is also one's own personal benefit.

To skillfully study the virtues of the Buddha is called "cultivating enlightenment" (*bodhi*); there are also sutras that speak of "cultivating the Buddha-path," which is merely a difference in translation.
“Abiding securely in the site of enlightenment” refers to the benefits obtained on the eighth stage and above.
The meaning of the “site of enlightenment” has been extensively explained as above.
To gradually train prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and to achieve realization upon entering the stages is termed “abiding securely.”
"To tread upon the tracks traversed by the Tathāgata" refers to the benefits obtained on the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Generally speaking, all wisdom, samādhis, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and dhāraṇīs are the tracks of the Buddha; thus, proceeding in accordance with these on the ten stages is called "treading.
Specifically, however, the final Vajropama-samādhi (Diamond-like Samādhi) is that which constitutes the Buddha's track.
This concludes the second section.
From here on follows the third, in which Śakra reveals his own offerings and protection so as to cause others to hold him in high esteem and respect.
This section contains two parts:
First, it clarifies that those who practice in accordance with the sūtras go to make offerings;

second, from the phrase "wherever [the sūtra is located]" onwards, it clarifies that one goes to protect the place where the sūtra resides, causing those who have not yet developed faith to do so, and providing protection for those who already possess it.
Above, Śakra praised the sutra and exhorted study;
below, the Buddha recounts and extols it.
"Excellent" is the general praise, while what follows is the specific exposition.
"According to what you have said" refers to the words themselves.
This means that the benefits of superior training mentioned in the preceding two sections of the sutra are entirely as the Emperor has spoken; thus, it is called "according to what you have said."
"I rejoice in your joy" is a statement of affirmation.
It affirms that the third type of practice mentioned above—providing offerings and protecting the site where the sutra is kept—is a great good; therefore, one rejoices in your joy.
"Er" is the same as "er" (thus).
From this point downward, the Tathāgata exhorts [the assembly] to study and circulate [this teaching].
Within this section, there are three parts:

First, this sutra explains that the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is taught herein; if there are those who receive, uphold, and make offerings to this sutra, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
2. From "Even if" (*sacet*) onwards, it clarifies that material offerings do not equal the cultivation of this sutra.
3. From "In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas" onwards, it cites actual events to provide proof.

At the beginning of this sutra, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment) of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present is explained in detail; thus, it clarifies that the sutra speaks of the Buddha.

The preceding "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetraparivarta*) clarifies the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāyakauśalyaparivarta*) clarifies the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body); and the "Chapter on Seeing Akṣobhya" (*Akṣobhyatathāgatasyavyūhanirdeśaparivarta*) clarifies the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* (dharma body)—this is what is termed the exposition of *bodhi*.

"From the words 'Therefore, O Lord of Devas, whether it be a man or a woman' onwards, it clarifies that those who receive, uphold, and make offerings to this sutra are thereby making offerings to the Buddha.
